Casting core analysis reveals production techniques and the diverse provenance of Shijia Cemetery’s bronze vessels

Shijia Cemetery and the adjacent Yucun Site are the first systematically excavated large-scale Zhou Dynasty (ca. 1046–256 BCE) funerary and settlement sites in eastern Longdong, Gansu Province, China. Bronzes from these sites show hybrid traits, blending Zhou culture traditions with Qin culture and Northern Steppe culture influences. This study examines the casting cores using petrography, major and trace elements, and REE and Sr isotopes. The analyses indicate that the casting core is primarily made of easily available loess without any temper or levigation. Rude Medium and miniature ritual vessels were cast locally from loess. By contrast, finely crafted miniature and large ritual vessels from medium tombs display distinct geochemical deviations, indicating non-local production. Although their specific provenance remains undetermined, these results not only indicate diverse sources of bronze metalwork in the Longdong region during the Zhou Dynasty but also reflect active intercultural exchange and the circulation of bronzes across the northwestern frontier.

The bronze civilization of the Shang and Zhou dynasties relied primarily on piece-mold casting technology. The following process is typically adopted when employing the clay mold casting technique. First, the model was made, and the clay molds were shaped over and around the positive model to create their negative ones. The casting core was then manufactured, and clay spacers or chaplets were fixed directly on the surface of the casting core to leave a gap between the molds and casting cores, allowing the molten metal to flow in. Before that, the molds were dried, baked, and spliced. Molten bronze was poured through the gating system to fill the cavity, and the subsequent removal of the broken molds and casting core revealed artifacts1,2. Although accessible and semi-exposed cores were usually removed during finishing, some cores were not cleaned, possibly because they were specifically used for funerary purposes and cleaning was unnecessary; therefore, they were retained. Permanently enclosed casting cores remain preserved within bronze artifacts. Regardless, the remaining casting cores have become important archaeological research materials for studying bronze production technologies and provenance.

In ancient bronze production, raw materials for clay molds and casting cores were typically procured locally, with discarded mold fragments accumulating as waste within the production areas. Crucially, when casting cores were retained within bronze artifacts due to incomplete removal during manufacturing, they were passively transported with the circulation of these objects, ultimately being buried in tombs or hoards3. Consequently, the casting cores preserved within the excavated bronzes retain both the lithological, geochemical, and elemental characteristics of the clay from their production sites, and information regarding the technical parameters of their fabrication4,5. Natural clay is formed by the physical, chemical, and biological weathering of loose parent material rocks on top of the pedestal rocks. Although the mineral and chemical constituents of clay are highly variable across regions owing to diverse factors in the soil-forming process, simulations confirm that firing leaves most elements, including major, trace, and rare earth elements (REE), largely unchanged, except for volatile elements (Br, S, Cl, As, and Sb)6,7,8,9,10. These REE signatures function as geochemical tracers11. Consequently, through an integrated analysis of major and trace elements, petrological characteristics, and REE signatures in the casting cores of bronze, it is possible to distinguish similarities and differences in provenance and identify potential source areas by means of geochemical tracing under certain circumstances10,12,13,14,15.

Academic research on casting cores in Shang and Zhou Dynasties in Chinese bronze artifacts has yielded significant methodological advancements. Holmes et al. systematically analyzed 112 casting cores from the Sackler Collection alongside soil samples from key Central Plains production sites. By applying multivariate statistics to compositional data, this study initiated the archaeometric analysis of Chinese bronze casting cores and established an empirical foundation for provenance research16.

Extant literature on the bronze casting provenance of the Shang and Zhou Dynasties through casting core analysis demonstrates a multidisciplinary advancement. One research team pioneered REE testing of casting molds, establishing REEs as robust tracers for identifying regional production differences17. Concurrently, another research team developed a phytolith assemblage analysis utilizing Jiuliandun Chu Tomb bronzes to demonstrate distinct phytolith signatures across stylistic groups, providing a tracing method independent of elemental analysis18. A research group integrated X-ray fluorescence (XRF), REE, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) data from the Panlongcheng and Xiangyang Chenpo Tombs, confirming local production in the mid-Yangtze region through geochemical affinity with local soils and pottery, contrasting sharply with Houma molds and southern laterite19. Similarly, a multi-method analysis (lithofacies, XRF, and ICP-AES) of Gaozhuang Tomb casting cores in Huaiyin identified mineralogical markers that are diagnostic of Chu-state casting traditions20.

Methodological refinements continue to evolve, as seen in Huang et al.’s studies on optimizing comparative models through XRD analysis of Xiangyang cemetery casting cores, such as those from Yugang and Shengang. Their elemental clustering clearly differentiated Yellow River production centers, such as Houma, from Yangtze centers, thus supporting the Eastern Zhou local casting hypotheses21. Wei Guofeng’s work on Jiuliandun casting cores combined polarized microscopy, XRD, XRF, and neutron activation analysis (NAA)22. This multi-technique approach revealed statistically significant differences in the mineralogy, chemistry, and phytoliths between local and imported bronzes23. Analysis of the clay cores of bronze artifacts unearthed from the Xiaxiangpu site showed that the raw materials of the clay cores came from the local area, while the source of the lead ore was the opposite, reflecting the different origins of the production areas and mineral materials24. Most recently, Ma Ding’s geochemical study of tomb casting cores from the Qiaojiayuan Spring and Autumn Period revealed southern laterite affinities distinct from those of northern loess. This finding provides material evidence for north-south metallurgical technological divergence25. Using petrographic and elemental analysis of cast cores, the origin of Sanxingdui bronzes was revealed26. Scholars have used casting cores and other methods to confirm that China’s earliest bronze horse sculptures were cast on the Loess Plateau27.

The studies of these scholars demonstrate that the geochemical and mineralogical analysis of bronze casting cores serves as one of the current methods for determining the provenance of bronze artifacts. These analyses employ XRF to determine the major and trace elements, combined with inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to analyze the REE distribution patterns. Integrating XRD with petrography characterizes the clay matrix mineral assemblages, whereas complementary biomarker characterization and phytolith morphology identify the raw material sources and manufacturing techniques. Currently, a considerable amount of analysis and testing data on pottery molds, casting cores, and clay from the production sites of the Shang and Zhou periods have been accumulated, providing comparable data for provenance studies.

Located in Xitou Village, Zaosheng Town, Ning County, Gansu Province, Shijia Cemetery is the first systematically excavated high-status Zhou dynasty necropolis in Longdong (eastern Gansu). The elite tombs M216 and M218 contained a ritual bronze assemblage featuring a seven-ding set and conclusive evidence of aristocratic status under the Zhou li ritual system. Mortuary evidence reveals that strict social hierarchies correlate with variability in grave goods. Collectively, the Shijia Cemetery and adjacent Yucun site establish a continuous archaeological sequence documenting cultural evolution in the upper Jing River Basin from Western Zhou through the Spring and Autumn periods. During Western Zhou’s hegemony, this strategic corridor functioned as a royal territory, exhibiting a canonical Zhou material culture. Following the transition to the Eastern Zhou period, Longdong became a contested frontier where Zhou-affiliated groups, Qin culture expansionists, and Rong pastoralists competed for territorial control, a geopolitical shift materially manifested in the hybrid bronze assemblages at both sites. The multi-political landscape of Eastern Longdong is materially encoded in Shijia’s bronze assemblages, revealing a hierarchical cultural synthesis wherein Zhou ritual traditions form the dominant framework integrated with Qin stylistic elements, Rong zoomorphic artistry, and Northern Steppe metallurgical techniques (Fig. 1a–g). Consequently, this cemetery provides pivotal archaeological evidence not only for reconstructing multi-piece mold casting technologies in the Zhou dynasty frontier workshops but also for analyzing power struggles among the Zhou, Qin, and Rong groups, while simultaneously tracing cultural transmission pathways across the Loess Plateau’s interregional contact zone.
Fig. 1: The photo shows artifacts of varying sizes, casting sophistication, and styles from the Shijia cemetery.

a Ding (Zhou Culture). b Ding (Qin Culture). c Gui (exquisitely cast small objects). d Ding (crudely cast miniature ritual vessels). e Ding (Artifacts combining Northern Steppes culture and Zhou culture). f Horse bit (Northern Steppes artifacts). g Tiger-shaped ornaments (Northern Steppes artifacts). h “Xianzi” li. i “Liangbo” spear.

Two inscribed bronze vessels excavated from the Shijia Cemetery—the “Xianzi” li and “Liangbo” spear — suggest potential origins of the Shijia population in the Qianhe River basin (Fig. 1h, i). The “Liangbo” spear likely entered the cemetery through Qin groups intermediaries following the Liang state’s collapse during the late Spring and Autumn period28. Further evidence of transregional connections was provided by excavating a sub-rectangular double-jointed horse bit with cheekpieces bearing thorn-shaped protrusions from Tomb M143 (Fig. 1f). Li Gang attributes such single- and double-jointed bits prevalent across northern China to the equestrian traditions of the Eurasian steppes, positing direct technological links to the early nomadic cultures of the Aral Sea littoral zone29.

The excavated ding exhibits distinct nomadic cultural affiliations (Fig. 1e), whereas variations in the bronze artifact dimensions and manufacturing quality collectively indicate complex provenance networks in the Shijia cemetery (Fig. 1d). This material evidence fundamentally reflects Eastern Longdong’s cultural evolution during the Zhou period, a dynamic synthesis integrating Zhou ritual systems, Qin-Rong political contestation, and Steppe technological diffusion. Bronze production networks in the borderland areas of eastern Gansu Province remain inadequately researched, particularly during the Zhou-Qin group transition period. Shijia Cemetery yielded numerous bronze artifacts with well-preserved casting cores, serving as critical physical evidence for the reconstruction of multi-piece mold casting operating chains. Through the compositional analysis (major/trace elements) and structural examination (porosity patterns) of these casting cores, the production sequences and technical standards can be restored. Their geochemical signatures provide direct provenance tracers while simultaneously elucidating complex resource networks and ethnic interaction mechanisms along Longdong’s eastern frontier during the Zhou-Qin group transition.

This study examined the production processes of casting cores and provenance characteristics of bronzes from the Shijia cemetery by analyzing 55 samples (Fig. 2; Appendix 1) spanning from the late Western Zhou through the mid-Spring and Autumn periods (ca. 850–550 BCE). The sample set comprised 41 bronze casting cores, including semi-exposed casting cores from ding-legs, retained composite-mold casting cores of complex configurations from gui-handles, and partially exposed casting cores from miniature objects retained after casting. The control group comprised six bronze clay ritual vessels (ding, gui, hu, and pan), which imitate bronze ritual forms and were produced by low-temperature baking or drying. Complementing these groups, the environmental baseline group incorporates eight samples from various contexts, including virgin soil, activity surfaces of house remains, and cultural layer soils.

Photos of some samples analyzed: From left to right, from top to bottom are bronze casting cores SJFT03-12, 14, 15, 20, 22, 23, 25, 28, 29, 30, 32, 36-38, 40, 41, and imitation bronze clay ritual vessel SJNL06.

During the sampling of bronze casting cores, the initial step involves distinguishing between the original casting cores and mixed tomb backfill sediments. Distinct color differences serve as the primary identification criteria, with casting cores exhibiting blue-gray or thermally oxidized red hues from high-temperature exposure and tomb backfill retaining homogeneous earthen-yellow primary sediments. Casting cores show material consolidation via high-temperature densification, increased hardness, and decreased porosity. Conversely, tomb backfills exhibit crumbly, loosely compacted structures that are easily deformable by hand. To mitigate burial contamination, surface stripping protocols were applied, in which the contaminated outer layers were mechanically removed using sterile scalpels to isolate the pristine internal matrices (Fig. 2). Analyses of major elements, mineral assemblages, and microstructural features, such as those obtained via SEM-EDS or XRD elucidate casting core production techniques. Furthermore, trace element geochemistry integrated with Rb-Sr isotopic signatures provides provenance discrimination of the casting origins.

During sampling, the samples were cut such that the mud core could be extracted in the form of solid blocks, and larger blocks of the samples were selected. Petrographic examination was conducted on 30 μm thin sections prepared from indurated casting cores blocks using a Leica DM2700P polarizing microscope to characterize mineral assemblages.

The samples were ground and pressed into tablets and then measured using a Bruker PUMA S2 energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (ED-XRF) equipped with an X-ray source operating at 40–50 kV tube voltage and 2 mA current, using a 28 mm spot diameter. Quantification was performed using a standard curve. A standard curve was established using 10 standard materials for ancient ceramic analysis developed by the Shanghai Institute of Ceramics, Chinese Academy of Sciences30,31, and the quantitative accuracy was verified using the C-7 standard material as a reference sample. Under these analytical conditions, the relative errors of the element measurements were less than 10%.
The crystalline structures of the clay minerals were analyzed using an Olympus portable X-ray diffractometer, which requires substantially smaller sample volumes than benchtop XRD systems.

Trace element analysis was performed using an Analytik Jena PlasmaQuant MS Elite inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer. First, a 200-mesh sample was oven-dried at 105 °C for 2–4 h. A 40 mg portion of the powdered sample was accurately weighed and placed in a Teflon cartridge. 0.5 mL of high-purity HNO3 and 1 mL of high-purity HF were slowly added, sequentially. The Teflon cartridge was placed in a steel sleeve, tightened, and then heated in a 190°C oven for at least 48 h. After the cartridge had cooled, the lid was opened and placed on a 150°C hot plate to dryness. 0.5 mL of HNO3 was then added and evaporated to dryness. This process was repeated. Then, 5 mL of 30% HNO3 was added, and the Teflon cartridge was again placed in the steel sleeve, tightened, and placed in a 150°C oven overnight. The solution was transferred to a polyethylene bottle, the Rh internal standard was added, and the sample was diluted to 100 g with 2% HNO3 for analysis. The accuracy for most trace elements was 5%.
Multiple Collector Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS)

Strontium isotope composition was measured using a Thermo Fisher Neptuneplus MC-ICP-MS instrument. The Strontium isotope instrument fractionation calibration used an exponential equation with 87Sr/86Sr = 8.375209.
Scanning electron microscope energy spectrum analysis (SEM-EDS)

The surface morphology and micro-area elemental composition were analyzed using a VEGA3 XMU SEM equipped with a Bruker Nano GmbH 610 M EDS at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV and a working distance of 15 mm. SEM-BSE imaging effectively identifies mineral phases (e.g., clay matrix, quartz, and carbonate) by mapping the atomic number contrast (Z-contrast) to grayscale values, providing microscopic evidence for the casting core raw material characteristics32. Subsequently, representative samples were selected for further analysis. Digital image analysis was performed using CT-AN software to extract the porosity parameters and segment the silt, sand, and clay matrix regions. Original BSE images were converted into binary data using ImageJ, excluding particles ≤6μm (Appendix 2). The area, Feret diameter, and roundness of each retained particle were calculated to construct a morphological dataset.
Lithofacies characteristics, microscopic characterization and physical statistics

Petrographic analysis enables the systematic characterization of raw materials and production techniques for bronze casting cores. A ternary diagram of porosity, silt, and clay was drawn (Fig. 3). According to the porosity, the proportions of silt sand, sand, and clay, combined with the petrographic characteristics and microstructure, can be divided into four groups.
Ternary diagram of extracted porosity, silt, sand, and clay.

Group A comprised samples SJFT01, SJFT03, SJFT08, and SJFT30, whereas Group B included samples SJFT05, SJFT07, SJFT09, SJFT32, and SJFT36. Both groups exhibit elevated silt and sand contents (44.7-59.2 wt%) relative to other groups. Porosity ranges from 10.7 wt% to 14.1 wt% in Group A, significantly lower than that of Group B (22.3–25.3 wt%). This disparity suggests that the Group A casting cores underwent more intensive compaction during production, thereby potentially contributing to reduced porosity. Petrographic analysis revealed that Groups A and B shared a low clay matrix content and minor carbonate mineral inclusions. Detrital minerals, predominantly quartz, K-feldspar, and plagioclase with subordinate muscovite (Fig. 4A, B), display moderate sorting and a subrounded morphology. The unimodal log-normal particle size distribution curves indicated the absence of intentional tempering additives. Given the similarities in composition and grain-size distribution to other groups, the raw materials for Groups A and B were probably unprocessed and sourced from silt-rich loess deposits such as near-surface or fluvial terrace sediments. Notably, Group A artifacts predominantly date to the Western Zhou period, whereas Group B contains materials from both the Western Zhou and the early Spring and Autumn periods (e.g., Tomb M4). This temporal distinction, combined with their compositional profiles, suggests spatially divergent sources for the casting core raw materials.
Fig. 4: Lithology and backscatter photos of casting core, virgin soil.

A From left to right, the SJFT09 lithofacies and backscattered photos. B From left to right, the SJFT14 lithofacies and backscattered photos. C From left to right, the SJTY07 lithofacies and backscattered photos. D From left to right, the SJFY21 lithofacies and backscattered photos.

Group C constituted the predominant category, representing 76% of the total casting core samples, including in-situ sediment samples extracted from archaeological contexts. This group comprised SJFT06, SJFT11, SJFT12, SJFT14, SJFT16, SJFT18, SJFT22, SJFT29, SJFT34, SJFT37, SJFT40, SJFT41, SJTY01, SJTY02, and SJTY07. The silt ratio ranges from 29 to 39 wt %, which was markedly lower than that of Groups A and B, whereas the relative clay matrix content was significantly higher (Fig. 4C). The detrital grains exhibited moderate sorting and subangular roundness. The mineralogical phases consisted primarily of quartz, K-feldspar, plagioclase, muscovite, and carbonate minerals with dominant silt-grade particles, classifying the material as silty clay. Under plane-polarized light, the clay matrix displayed a uniform brown-yellow coloration and calcareous composition, with a narrow particle size distribution. The absence of coarse detrital minerals indicates a provenance from a stable sedimentary environment, consistent with the homogeneous structural characteristics of the aeolian loess deposits33.

Group D comprised casting core sample SJFT21 and imitation bronze clay ritual vessels (SJNL01–SJNL05). These imitations exhibited an elevated clay matrix content (61 wt% on average), conferring superior plasticity. Characterized by low porosity and reduced silt and sand fractions relative to the local virgin soil and other casting cores, the samples displayed angular particles with distinct silt-grade edges and poor sorting (Fig. 4D). This high clay content and low porosity may be conducive to the shaping of fine imitation bronze patterns. However, it also requires more precise drying and roasting control to avoid cracking. Elutriation leads to clay loss, quartz enrichment, and a significant increase in the quartz-to-feldspar ratio. The scarcity of coarse sand indicates the selection of original high-clay layers (such as paleosols) without levigation. The particles are angular and poorly sorted, which may reflect short-distance transport or weak hydrodynamic transformations. Combined with the characteristics of low calcium content in some parts, the main body conforms to the characteristics of paleosol layers in aeolian sedimentary sequences.

Groups A and B had a relatively low clay matrix content and slightly higher proportions of silt and fine sand than the other groups, but their compositions and particle size distributions did not differ significantly from those of the other groups. The particle size exhibited a unimodal log-normal distribution pattern, indicating the absence of a temper. Deep artificial levigation reduces not only the contents of Al2O3, TiO2, but also elements such as Na2O, MgO, K2O, CaO, Fe2O3, and the proportion of finer particles34. These characteristics suggested that the raw material was derived directly from silt-rich sediments without levigation. The majority of the bronze casting mud cores correspond to Group C, displaying mineralogical composition, silt content, and porosity values consistent with local soil properties. The analytical results confirmed the absence of deliberate sand tempering, implying the direct utilization of local soils without specialized treatment. Conversely, imitation bronze ritual clay vessels are predominantly associated with Group D, which is characterized by a significantly higher clay matrix content. Despite this enrichment, persistent quartz silt particles indicate the targeted utilization of specific sedimentary layers (e.g., paleosols) within the aeolian loess-paleosol sequences.

Collectively, the four sample groups exhibit predominantly silt-grade particles (10–60μm), with unimodal log-normal grain-size distributions and scarce coarse sand. This pattern precludes a proximal alluvial influence, aligns with aeolian distal sedimentation characteristics, and reflects advanced source material weathering. Grain-size statistics confirmed insignificant intergroup distribution differences, and petrographic analysis revealed no evidence of a deliberate temper. Coupled with the unimodal log-normal distributions, this definitively excludes the deliberate addition of size-graded admixtures. Given the homogeneous grain-size distributions, consistent mineralogical compositions, and the absence of tempering indicators, all groups were likely derived from natural aeolian sediments (loess) without levigation or intensive processing. Consequently, production of casting cores essentially constituted direct loess utilization. Nevertheless, these shared petrographic attributes preclude reliable differentiation of artifact casting sites based solely on extant data.

Casting cores SJFT30, SJFT34, and SJFT40 exhibit laminar structures. For instance, SJFT30 displayed an outer fine clay slip layer (approximately 3 mm thick) and an inner coarse silt-rich layer containing lead corrosion products from artifacts (Fig. 5c). SJFT32 and SJFT36 featured calcareous layers admixed with minor quartz particles (Fig. 5e, f). Such stratification and surface coatings are predominantly observed in large Early Spring and Autumn period vessels, particularly in artifacts from Tomb M216. Some samples showed traces of plant remains mixed in, with minerals and voids distributed in the same orientation, suggesting that they were pounded or compacted. (Fig. 5a, b, d). During the late Shang period, vessel casting cores were typically coated with fine clay-based slips, whereas chariot weapon casting cores employed sand tempering35. The application of fine surface coatings has also been reported in the Yinxu mud cores36. Specialized coatings containing calcined bone and calcite were utilized at the Houma foundry37,38. Chastain identified lime particles on mold surfaces in Zhouyuan (Shaanxi) and proposed three functional roles for these coatings: facilitating the clean separation of cast objects to ensure smooth surfaces, protecting mold integrity during casting, and serving as sacrificial layers for repair or replacement39.

a, b Suspected plant remains. c SJFT30 shows stratification, with the outer layer being a fine mud layer affected by lead corrosion. d SJFT29 shows consistent mineral and pore orientation after tampering. e, f SJFT32 shows a high-calcium layer.

The application of the fine surface layer of the casting cores in the Shijia cemetery is consistent with the purpose of “applying fine mud” in Yinxu to optimize the surface quality of the castings. However, most are closed-casting cores, likely reflecting a tradition of producing casting cores for internal cavities. For internal closed casting cores, this practice may offer limited functional benefits because no significant differences were observed between the internal, semi-closed, and closed casting cores. However, the cause of the high calcium layer (artificial application or burial formation) still needs further verification, although there is a technical tradition of artificial application. Overall, the Shijia casting cores were predominantly clay-based without a sand temper, suggesting the direct use of loess. Their relatively loose texture and good collapsibility, combined with high calcium and low silicon contents, satisfy the functional requirements for casting cores.

The major elements in 40 samples (28 casting cores, 7 virgin soils, 5 activity surfaces of house remains, and soil samples of the cultural layer) were analyzed by XRF (Appendix 3). Copper (0.5–6.4 wt%, avg. 2.3 wt%) and lead (0.1–17.8 wt%, avg. 2.4 wt%) were consistently detected in the casting cores, whereas both elements were below the detection limits in virgin soil, stratigraphic sediments, and clay ritual vessels. Cu and Pb originating from metal infiltration during casting or from post-depositional corrosion were excluded from the raw material provenance analysis of the casting core. Lead enrichment in the casting cores significantly exceeds that of Sn because of its lower volatility relative to Sn, which facilitates vapor deposition in mold cavities. PbO reacts with clay silicates to form a viscous, lead-rich glass, which enhances the mechanical retention of metal oxides40. The lower retention of Cu relative to that of Pb is related to its higher solubility, forming soluble complexes that are susceptible to leaching in burial environments41.

The 26 casting core samples exhibited high levels of Al, Ca, and Fe, but extremely low levels of P, Ti, and Mn, followed by low levels of Na, Mg, and K. Among them, sample SJFT16 was anomalous, containing 19.6 wt% Si, 11.9 wt% Pb, and 18.2 wt% Fe, respectively. Its original composition could not be determined because of the significant infiltration of either Pb corrosion products from the post-depositional processes or metallic Pb from the casting. Consequently, SJFT16 was excluded from the subsequent compositional analysis.

The oxide composition of the samples was characterized by the following ranges and averages: SiO2 (53.2–63.6 wt%, avg. 58.8 wt%), Al2O3 (12.9–16.4 wt%, avg. 15.6 wt%), CaO (6.5–15.6 wt%, avg. 10.5 wt%), Fe2O3 (5.6–13.0 wt%, avg. 6.8 wt%), MgO (2.6–3.7 wt%, avg. 3.1 wt%), K2O (2.2–4.3 wt%, avg. 2.9 wt%), and Na2O (0–2.9 wt%, avg. 1.0 wt%). Elements below 1 wt% were excluded. Among these oxides, SiO2, Al2O3, and CaO exhibit the largest variations, while others show smaller fluctuations. For comparison, loess, which dominates the Yellow River Basin in northern China, typically has the highest contents of SiO2, Al2O3, and CaO, followed by Fe2O3, MgO, and K2O; Na2O, TiO2, and MnO contents are very low. Specifically, northern loess compositions fall within these ranges: SiO2 (48.2–63.5 wt%), TiO2 (0.1–0.9 wt%), Al2O3 (7.8–14.6 wt%), Fe2O3 (2.2–6.1 wt%), FeO (0.5–2.2 wt%), MnO ( < 0.4 wt%), MgO ( < 6.6 wt%), CaO (3.5–19.9 wt%), Na2O (2.0–2.3 wt%), and K2O (0.2–2.4 wt%). By contrast, laterite, which is prevalent in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River in southern China, has notably low contents of elements, such as Ca and Mg. Consequently, the major element composition differed markedly between the two soil types42,43. Analysis of virgin soil, activity surfaces of house remains, and soil samples from the cultural layer. The Shijia cemetery site showed Ca contents ranging from 7.6 wt% to 14.7 wt% and Fe contents between 7.2 wt% and 7.4 wt%. The distribution patterns of major elements revealed slight fluctuations in the contents of Al2O3, Fe2O3, and CaO, with other elements exhibiting minor variations. Loess is characterized by major oxides in decreasing abundance: SiO2, Al22O3, CaO, Fe2O3, MgO, K2O, and Na2O; the contents of other elements are relatively low. The elemental distribution observed in the casting cores conformed to this loess pattern.

The soil samples included surface soil from the ruins of a Zhou Dynasty house, four excavated cultural layers, and three raw soil samples collected from the site. XRD analysis revealed that the main mineral phases in these samples were quartz, calcite, feldspar, muscovite, and minor primary minerals (Fig. 6a).
Fig. 6: The XRD spectra for the samples.
a Activity surfaces of house remains, and soil samples of cultural layer. b Casting Cores.

The carbonates in the loess of the eastern Longdong area are primarily composed of calcite and dolomite. Its high calcium content results from the significant enrichment of carbonate minerals18. Loess typically contains silt-sized, rounded calcite particles, the abundance of which is positively correlated with CaCO3 content. Some of these calcite particles are primary, while others are secondary carbonates formed by atmospheric precipitation, groundwater, and biological activity. The ratio of primary to secondary carbonates is controlled by climate aridity: higher aridity corresponds to higher CaCO3 content. For instance, CaCO3 content in the Malan loess of the Yellow River’s middle reaches increases from southeast to northwest. Within the study area, both soil samples from the cultural layers and virgin soil consisted of typical loess situated within the casting core distribution zone of the Loess Plateau.

Casting cores excavated from the Shijia cemetery were analyzed using XRD (Fig. 6b). The main phases identified were quartz, calcite, feldspar, and muscovite, which is consistent with the mineralogical composition of the local loess reference samples. Notably, chlorite was detected in sample SJFT22 but not in the other casting cores. The roundness and particle size distribution of the chlorite particles within this sample differed from those in the other casting cores. For SJFT25, the calcite diffraction peak was either weak or absent. Two explanations have been proposed for this observation. First, loess undergoes varying degrees of leaching and sedimentation during soil formation, resulting in different calcite contents at different accumulation depths. Even within the same location, the calcite content varied with specific sampling points. Second, the casting core may have been exposed to high temperatures during casting. Calcite decomposes when heated to 850–900 °C, which weakens or eliminates its XRD diffraction peak. For comparison, casting cores from bronze artifacts excavated in the loess area of the Western Zhou Dynasty cemetery in Hengshui, Shanxi, were also analyzed44. The main phase compositions of the four samples analyzed were relatively consistent, comprising quartz, feldspar, muscovite, and calcite, which is consistent with typical loess characteristics.
Test results of rare earth and trace elements

The results of REE and trace element analyses of the casting cores, raw soil, and imitation bronze clay ritual vessels are presented in Appendices 4, 5, and 6. Chondrite-normalized REE distribution patterns for these samples reveal consistent characteristics: the patterns for all samples were subparallel, exhibiting an “L”-shaped profile with a right-leaning negative slope45. Light REEs (LREEs) were enriched relative to heavy REEs (HREEs), and the degree of fractionation was uniform across samples. Specifically, the patterns show steep slopes from La to Eu and gentler slopes from Eu to Lu. Eu values cluster around 0.60, indicating a distinct negative Eu anomaly. By contrast, the Ce values were clustered near 1.00, showing no significant anomalies, as illustrated in Fig. 7a. This pattern is typical of felsic rocks in the continental crust46. Significant negative Eu anomalies indicate widespread fractional crystallization of plagioclase during magma evolution7,47. Ce/Ce values close to 1.00 indicate that diagenesis occurred in a relatively reducing environment, without undergoing oxidation processes similar to marine environments48,49. The REE model indicated that its provenance was a continental upper crust environment.
a Rare earth element distribution pattern. b Triangular diagram of REE characteristic parameters of casting core.

The microstructural characteristics, major element composition, and REE distribution patterns collectively demonstrated that the casting cores originated from loess materials. The vertical variation in the REE characteristic parameters throughout the stratigraphic profile reveals distinct material sources and paleoenvironmental conditions50. This disparity is effectively demonstrated by the triangular diagram illustrating deviations of ΣLREE/ΣHREE ratios from mean values (Fig. 7b). The δEu anomalies primarily reflect source rock lithology, exhibiting differential magnitudes owing to varied diagenetic histories, whereas δCe anomalies were modulated by paleoclimatic conditions and post-depositional geochemical processes. The absolute deviation magnitude of ΣLREE/ΣHREE from the mean value quantitatively represents light-to-heavy REE fractionation intensity.

Analytical results show confined sample distributions within the diagram, indicating limited δEu and δCe variability with relative geochemical invariance. Minor variations in REE parameters among the casting cores suggest genetic similarity of the loess derived from aeolian deposits containing materials from multiple provenance regions under atmospheric transport. The proximity of the absolute deviation values of LREE/HREE between the two local virgin soil horizons delineates a representative source of autochthonous loess accumulation. By contrast, significant deviations in ΣLREE/ΣHREE between casting cores and local virgin soil imply differing depositional climates and formation processes for partial loess materials, reflecting environmental influences and source heterogeneity. This complexity may arise from the stratigraphic variability or diverse raw material provenances.
Strontium isotope test results and analysis

Strontium (Sr) has four naturally occurring isotopes: 88Sr, 87Sr, 86Sr, and 84Sr. The isotope 87Sr is produced by the radioactive decay of 87Rb. Differences in the geochemical behaviors of rubidium (Rb) and strontium (Sr) result in Sr enrichment in silicic magmatic rocks. Over geological time, 87Rb decays to 87Sr. Consequently, older silicic rocks exhibit higher concentrations of 87Sr and thus higher 87Sr/86Sr ratios. These ratios provide valuable information for constraining the geological sources. The chemical weathering of the Earth’s surface occurs under low-temperature conditions that do not cause significant strontium isotope fractionation. Therefore, the strontium released during rock weathering, once thoroughly mixed within the hydrosphere and biosphere, reflects the 87Sr/86Sr signature of its source rocks51,52.

Strontium isotope analysis (Appendix 7) shows local virgin soil values of 0.715 to 0.716, establishing the local isotopic signature. Chronologically, casting core data can be divided into three groups relative to this local baseline (Fig. 8), Group A (87Sr/86Sr ≥ 0.716), Group B (0.715 <87Sr/86Sr <0.716), and Group C (87Sr/86Sr ≤ 0.715). Group B contained the most data points, encompassing most casting cores used for bronze casting. Group B constituted the predominant signature, representing 64.3% of the casting cores strontium isotope ratios. These values exhibit ratios identical to those of the local virgin soil, indicating the consistent utilization of indigenous materials. Group B spans from the late Western Zhou to the early Spring and Autumn periods. As all local soils fall within Group B, this signature likely represents locally sourced materials used continuously in casting core production. Given that all the tested site-specific virgin soil falls within Group B, this isotopic signature represents the soil continuously employed in casting core production at the cemetery. Only locally or proximally sourced soils could maintain this specific geochemical signature across such a prolonged temporal duration. Consequently, the Group B materials were likely derived from the immediate vicinities of the casting sites.

Group A shows significantly higher 878787878787Sr/86Sr ratios than Group B, whereas Group C exhibits lower ratios than Group B. Group A mainly comprised imitation bronze clay ritual vessels, suggesting that certain artifacts have distinct Sr isotopic signatures. The XRF data further revealed that specific imitation bronze clay ritual vessels (SJNL01, SJNL02, and SJNL03) showed less compositional similarity to others, with some exhibiting low calcium content, suggesting a special origin. Whether these characteristics arise from differences in production processes requires further investigation.

Samples in Group C exhibit lower 87Sr/86Sr ratios. This group primarily comprised artifacts from tombs M6, M218, and M216. M6 is a miniature artifact cast exquisitely. M216 and M218 are large tombs, and the analyzed artifacts from them are large ding. M216 is a high-level tomb dating back to the early Spring and Autumn period. The shape of its tripod(s) is similar to that of artifacts such as Xuanwang 42nd Year Ding and Jinhou Bangfu Ding (from Tomb I11M64:130 at the Northern Zhao Jinhou Cemetery, late Western Zhou). However, M216 dates to the early Spring and Autumn period, and its artifact style and 87Sr/86Sr ratio differ from those characteristic of the local region. Tomb M218, dating to the mid-Spring and Autumn periods, features ding displaying a strong Qin cultural style. As a higher-level tomb, its artifact style and inferred production location differ from the local norms. This suggests that with the cultural influence and northward migration of the Qin people, artifacts produced elsewhere were brought to the area and buried in the tomb. From late Western Zhou through Eastern Zhou to the early Spring and Autumn period, Group B maintained a stable source of casting materials. The casting cores in this group originated from crudely cast miniaturized ritual vessels, indicating that these objects were locally cast and reflected regional bronze-casting traditions.

Provenance analysis utilizes compositional signatures that integrate trace elements and 87Sr/86Sr in casting cores, with complementary data from archaeological context and typological-stylistic analysis. According to geochemical theory, for a group of rock or mineral samples formed simultaneously from the same source, the ratios of 87Rb/86Sr and 87Sr/86Sr form a straight line, called an isochron. The isochron intercept reflects the initial 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio of the geological body. The isochron can be used to infer the age of the geological body and can also be used for tracing53. Analogously, 87Sr/86Sr covariation in ceramics sourced from homogeneous clay deposits establishes an analytical framework for tracing the provenance of bronze casting cores54. Critically, bronze casting cores preserve the source geochemical signatures because they avoid high-temperature alterations. Measured 87Rb/86Sr and 87Sr/86Sr ratios from three artifact categories—crudely cast miniatures, finely cast miniatures, and bulk ritual vessels—reveal robust isochron relationships specifically among crudely cast miniatures (Fig. 9a). Their clustered distribution indicated closely related soil sources and shared production origins for the corresponding casting cores. Notably, the bulk ritual vessel M38, with an analogous crudely cast aligns isotopically with this miniature group. Conversely, imitation bronze clay ritual vessels exhibit dispersed strontium isotopic signatures, a pattern corroborated in Fig. 9b (87Sr/8686Sr versus 1/Sr plot).

REE analysis plots the total REE content against the LREE/HREE ratios in scatter diagrams (Fig. 10a). Although the samples showed dispersed distributions overall, there was a subset of clusters with local soil samples. Notably, the miniature ritual vessels and the crudely cast medium-sized ritual vessel from Tomb M38 exhibited a clustered distribution, mirroring strontium and rubidium isotopic patterns discussed earlier. Chronologically, artifacts from the late Western Zhou and mid-Spring and Autumn periods demonstrated significant temporal clustering, with no marked divergence between these phases (Fig. 10b).

Trace element data were log-transformed to stabilize variance and mitigate heteroscedasticity while preserving intrinsic properties and correlations, a process that concurrently compresses variable scales through non-linear scaling. The trace elements selected for principal component analysis (PCA) in this study excluded Ti, Cu, Sn, Mn, Rb, and Sr. Titanium and manganese were excluded because they are abundant in soil and were thus not considered at trace levels. Copper and tin exhibit high contents in the casting core, as revealed by the XRF analysis, and these elements are prone to mixing during the casting process or subsequent burial, leading to their exclusion from the analysis. Rubidium and strontium were omitted because their isotopes and contents are discussed separately in this work.
PCA analysis of trace elements in clay samples after logarithmic transformation.

In summary, the following trace elements were selected for analysis: Li, Be, Sc, V, Cr, Co, Ni, Ga, Y, Zr, Nb, Mo, Cs, and Ba. PCA of these trace elements (Fig. 11) indicated that the miniature ritual vessels exhibited strong clustering and that their elemental composition resembled that of the local soil. By contrast, high-grade large ritual vessels from tombs M216 and M218 show a relatively scattered distribution, differing significantly from crudely cast medium-sized ritual vessels, miniature ritual vessels, and local soil. The imitation bronze clay ritual vessels also display a scattered distribution. While some are compositionally close to the local soil, the group as a whole shows no significant compositional differences across different time periods. These trace element findings are consistent with the results of strontium isotope and REE analyses.
Principal component analysis of casting molds and cores and virgin soil from bronze casting sites in various regions during the Shang and Zhou dynasties.

Integrated analysis of trace elements, REE, and strontium isotopes reveals consistent evidence for non-local provenance of the exquisitely cast small ritual vessels and high-grade large ritual vessels (M216 and M218) alongside the exquisitely cast M6 miniature artifact, indicating external introduction (where “local casting” denotes production within the surrounding regions of Longdong area, given the current absence of identified foundry sites in this territory). Conversely, the crudely cast miniature and medium-sized M38 vessels exhibited isotopic and elemental signatures compatible with local or proximal manufacturing origins.

To further investigate the potential north-south differences in bronze casting production areas, analytical data from casting cores and molds were compared. Data from casting molds for bronze casting cores, soil samples from bronze casting sites, and bronze casting cores analyzed across various regions during the Shang and Zhou dynasties were compiled (Appendix 8). To ensure comparability of the data, PCA was performed using XRF test results for the commonly measured major element oxides: Na2O, MgO, Al2O3, SiO2, K2O, CaO, Fe2O3, and TiO2 (Fig. 12).

Currently, Hubei and Anhui provinces contribute the most to the data points. Although the data points were relatively scattered, concentrated clusters were evident above the origin of the PCA plot. These clusters correspond to the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, where the local soil is typically laterite. These laterites were classified as low-calcium clays, reflecting the characteristics of southern China’s laterites. By contrast, Gansu and Shanxi are positioned in the upper left quadrant of Fig. 12, showing virtually no overlap with the Yangtze River basin clusters. This region is predominantly characterized by loess, indicating the use of loess-derived materials. Some data points in Henan and Anhui are clustered below the origin in Fig. 12. Geographically situated between the loess and laterite regions, some data points from Henan overlap with a limited number of points from both regions.

The statistical comparison above indicates that while PCA of casting cores cannot precisely pinpoint the casting origin, it reveals discernible north-south differences at a regional scale. This regional distinction is exemplified by the typically high calcium content of northern loess. Consequently, the major element compositions can reflect broad-scale geographical variations, such as the contrast between the northern (loess) and southern (laterite) regions. However, this approach lacks diagnostic value for determining whether a specific bronze assemblage originates from the same workshop or different workshops.

Casting cores recovered from the vicinity of the Shijia cemetery and Liujiawa residential area in Chengcheng consistently demonstrated elevated CaO content55. This characteristic aligns with the high calcium levels identified in the Shaanxi paleosols and parallels the significant calcium content documented in Houma pottery molds from the middle Yellow River region56. Such elevated calcium constitutes a diagnostic characteristic of pottery molds and casting cores excavated throughout the loess-dominated regions of the Gansu, Shanxi, and Shaanxi Provinces. This phenomenon originates from the abundant microcrystalline calcite within the calcareous clay matrices, which forms intimate associations with clay minerals. Although sedimentation and leaching processes may reduce the bulk CaO content, they negligibly modify the inherent CaO composition of the clay fraction. Consequently, casting cores and pottery molds manufactured using loess retained characteristically high residual calcium signatures.

Current accumulations of REE data from Shang-Zhou pottery molds and casting cores (Appendix 9) enabled a comparative analysis. Plotting total ΣREE against LREE/HREE ratios reveals partial overlap between the Shijia cemetery dataset and the dispersed Houma pottery mold signatures in Fig. 13. The Houma Jin State bronze-casting complex encompasses four key sites: the Jindu Xintian site, Niucun Ancient City locations II and XXII, and the Baidian workshop. These operations were chronologically clustered within the late Spring and Autumn to the early Warring States period (ca. 550–380 BCE). Although definitive technological connections between the Shijia cemetery and Houma casting sites remain unverified, their geochemical convergence suggests probable clay procurement from loess deposits within analogous pedogenic environments.

The principal trace elements, rare earth distribution patterns, phase characteristics, and mineral compositions of bronze casting cores from the Shijia cemetery exhibited mineralogical and geochemical affinities with loess deposits. This consistency indicates the utilization of unprocessed natural loess without artificial admixtures such as plant ash or coarse sand, suggesting that the production of casting cores occurred within the loess distribution zones. Integrating research on Yucun’s pottery industry, where a specialized labor division produced fine paste and sand tempered wares, reveals that casting cores directly exploited raw loess without requiring sophisticated processing, such as ceramic production57. The characteristically elevated calcium signatures in the casting cores match the geochemical fingerprint of northern Chinese loess, which is diametrically opposed to the southern lateritic systems. The enriched primary calcite in loess enables calcium to serve as a robust diagnostic proxy for distinguishing northwestern loess from southern laterite provenance. However, its limited discriminatory power for intra-regional workshop differentiation necessitates complementary strontium isotopic analysis integrated with trace element and REE profiling.

A comprehensive multi-provenance analysis indicated that bronze artifacts from the Shijia cemetery are derived from both local production and external sources. This mixed-source model materially reflects the polycentric power dynamics and cross-cultural engagement in bronze production and circulation within the Longdong region, occurring against the backdrop of the Zhou Royal Court’s declining authority. This duality is further evidenced by tomb hierarchies. Elite tombs such as M216 and M218 exhibit externally sourced ritual vessels, while stylistic and technological analyses reveal diversified craft traditions in their artifacts. The early Spring and Autumn period Tomb M216 contained seven ding and six gui food containers – markers of status aligned with Zhou ritual norms – alongside numerous locally produced miniature ritual vessels. These crudely crafted funerary objects featured hollow-cast bottoms and sealed openings, reflecting simplified casting techniques. Rather than representing cultural “degeneration,” this dual assemblage of prestige and miniature ritual objects demonstrates dynamic adaptation of burial practices under constraints of resources, technology, and cultural identity. Such innovations provide critical insights into the maintenance of ritual systems and sociocultural strategies in marginal communities.

Tomb M218, dated to the mid-Spring and Autumn periods, likely belonged to an elite figure known as Xianzi, and was interred with seven ding and eight gui food containers. The tomb’s elevated status suggests that its occupants represented a Qin culture-affiliated aristocratic group. The artifact assemblage displays strong Qin culture characteristics, indicative of external influences potentially originating from core Qin territories or state-managed distribution networks. The pervasive presence of Qin culture elements during this phase signified regional control through the centralized control of ritual bronzes, with Xianzi’s group exemplifying Qin’s territorial administration. Dietary analysis further revealed socioeconomic stratification in which individuals in elite burials consumed significantly more animal protein than commoners who relied primarily on millet agriculture. This nutritional disparity, which extends from subsistence practices to ritual vessel consumption, demonstrates how status differentiation permeates multiple dimensions of life58.

During the early Spring and Autumn periods, the proto-porcelain excavated from Tomb M6 represents a rare discovery in northwestern China, indicating diversified procurement channels of funerary objects. Bronze artifacts predominantly comprised finely cast miniature items. The ding and gui food containers exhibited stylistic variations spanning a spectrum from crude to refined casting techniques. These miniatures maintained forms identical to their counterparts in the Central Plains Guo State cemetery, confirming the preservation of Zhou dynasty stylistic traditions. Provenance studies also established their external origins. Tomb M38 from the mid-Spring and Autumn periods displays strong Qin culture elements, demonstrating Qin-influenced local bronze production with distinctive innovations. For example, the unearthed ding-style vessel integrates steppe pottery forms with Zhou-style ornamentation, providing material evidence for technological exchange between the Qin culture and the northwestern frontier communities. This attests to the existence of cross-political technological networks.

Abundant crudely cast miniatures epitomize localized production techniques adapted to regional conditions. Such crudely cast miniatures are primarily distributed across the Central Plains, Jin state territories, and Guanlong regions, appearing in tombs associated with the Zhou, Qin, Rui, Wei, and Guo polities. Their increased prevalence in eastern areas corroborates the transmitted texts documenting the sociopolitical upheaval during the Zhou Court’s eastward relocation (770 BCE). Western political centers were abandoned, causing displaced Zhou elites to lose ancestral land and hereditary ritual bronzes. Under new political configurations, resources previously controlled by Western Zhou royalty diminished significantly, creating unprecedented constraints on ritual bronze production in the early Spring and Autumn period59. The Shijia cemetery’s crudely cast bronze vessels represent locally produced funerary items rather than imports. Characterized by crude casting and minimal decoration, they differ functionally from ritual bronze. Their production met low-cost funerary needs while embodying the concept of serving the dead as if they were alive.

During the Early Spring and Autumn periods, tombs M6 and M216 contained fine imported ritual objects, while simultaneously demonstrating the tacitly permitted local production of medium- and low-tier burial goods. By contrast, during the mid-Spring and Autumn periods, under the dominance of the Qin culture, a clear shift occurred. As seen in tomb M218, the ruling authority monopolized the distribution rights of high-status ritual vessels. These elite tombs exclusively contained large imported ritual objects, with no small locally produced items. However, contemporaneous tomb M38 reveals distinctly Qin culture artifacts that were locally produced yet stylistically influenced by multiple craft traditions, revealing the complex interactions, choices, and dynamic integration among three key groups within the region’s mortuary practices: the ruling elite, local artisan communities possessing specialized technical skills (technical communities), and declining indigenous nobility striving to maintain traditional practices.

Bronze artifacts from Shijia Cemetery demonstrate multiple provenances, including locally and adjacently produced items and long-distance imports. This reflects the sophisticated material exchange networks maintained in this region during periods of upheaval. Artifacts from different sources represent distinct production technologies, with locally made items being more refined than imported ones. Refined imports are likely to represent more advanced techniques or different craft traditions.

This multiplicity of origins and complexity of technological exchange epitomizes the characteristics of frontier zones situated at cultural crossroads and political contestation during specific historical periods, particularly the waning Zhou authority and the Qin-Rong rivalry. It provides concrete material evidence and scientific support for understanding such cross-cultural interactions between the Zhou, Qin, Rong, and northern steppe cultures. The pattern of bronze provenance, where locally produced low-tier utilitarian objects coexisted with externally sourced high-status ritual vessels, indirectly reflects the fragmented political landscape, the infiltration of multiple powers, and potentially constrained or pragmatically oriented local technology in the frontier regions following the decline of royal Zhou control.

Through high-resolution geochemical provenance analysis of casting cores from Shijia bronzes combined with conventional archaeological methods, this study clearly revealed a dual-source pattern during the late Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn periods in eastern Gansu’s frontier region. This pattern comprises locally or adjacently produced crude utilitarian objects along with externally imported refined prestige goods. This discovery robustly demonstrates the heightened diversity in bronze provenance and the significant complexity in the underlying networks of technological exchange and material circulation within this region against the complex historical backdrop of declining Zhou power and the Qin-Rong comminicate. It provides valuable empirical evidence and a scientific basis not only for understanding the Shijia cemetery itself but also for exploring cross-cultural material exchange and social dynamics within ancient Chinese frontier zones during periods of political transition and ethnic interaction.

Future research should expand the databases of strontium isotopes, trace elements, and REEs to construct geochemical fingerprints of the Loess Plateau. Supplementing samples from Guanzhong and southern Shanxi would quantify the impact of the Qin culture’s eastward expansion on production networks. Studies of casting cores confirmed that Longdong functioned not as a peripheral backwater but as a vibrant bronze exchange hub. This role combined Zhou ritual resilience with frontier innovation, which is essential for understanding early multicultural integration in China. Integrating lead isotope provenance data with casting core data would establish a tripartite framework for analyzing ore sources, casting techniques, and circulation networks, thereby reconstructing bronze production chains.
